title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: Never argue with the tape. A great company in a Stage 4 markdown is a falling knife until institutions finish distributing and build a proper Stage 1 floor.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis Discipline

web_blocks.html: Uber's business earned a COMPOUNDER_PASS in our blind fundamental audit. However, the technical tape sends a clear warning. At the November 17, 2026 close of $68.81 (-1.69% on the day), Uber sits in Stan Weinstein Stage 4 (Markdown) (`STAGE4_BELOW_STRUCTURAL_FLOOR`, gate `CAP_REJECTED`) [21, 24]. Shares are down 25.84% from their $92.78 high and -24.64% over the past year [21]. Price remains below every key trendline: -0.72% below the 50-day SMA ($69.31), -5.16% below the 200-day SMA ($72.55), -4.35% below the 30-week SMA ($71.94), and -0.91% below the 10-week EMA ($69.44) [21, 24].

Weekly (`1W`), Daily (`1D`), and 4-Hour (`4H`) charts confirm that buyers lack control [24]. Uber hovers just above its 20-day SMA ($68.08), yet its -1.69% drop on November 17 came on 22.22 million shares [21]. That equals 1.27x the 30-day average volume of 17.53 million shares, showing active institutional supply [21]. Momentum readings stay weak across all timeframes: Daily RSI is 49.11, Weekly RSI is 44.99, and 4H RSI is 48.38 [24]. ATR-14 is $2.08 and Bollinger Band width is 10.84% [24]. Meanwhile, the US market sits in a Downtrend with 42.6% breadth above the 50DMA, 7 distribution days, and a 5.12% 10-year yield [23]. Buying a Stage 4 stock mid-air carries poor short-term odds.

web_blocks.html: Our deterministic options scan (`options_snapshot.py`) aligns with the equity tape [24]. Uber's 30-day ATM implied volatility (IV) is 37.5% versus 32.0% HV20, placing the chain in an IV_ELEVATED regime (`WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT_OR_BASE`) [24]. Buying naked short-dated calls at $68.81 is a theta trap below the 50-day and 200-day averages. Only if Uber tests its $64.04 shelf and stabilizes should traders deploy the Jan 15, 2027 (59 DTE) $67.5 / $77.5 Bull Call Debit Spread [24]. You buy the $67.5 Call at $4.83 mid (OI 4,294) and sell the $77.5 Call at $1.10 mid (OI 7,477) for a $3.73 net debit [24]. Max loss is $373.00 (45.0 bps of $82,808.19 actual net worth, or 37.3 bps on the $100,000 reference-NAV denominator used in the deterministic options table), max profit is $627.00 (1.68:1 R:R), and breakeven is $71.23 (+3.52%) [24]. Net delta is +$36.10 per $1 move, while theta decay is just -$1.25/day. Close at 65%–75% of max profit ($438.90 gain) or exit early below $64.04 [24].

Two technical paths can flip Uber from `CAP_REJECTED` to `CLEAR_FOR_CONSIDERATION`. First, price can test the $62.00–$65.00 support zone ($64.04 low and $62.17 Pivot S1), dry up on selling volume, and form a 4H higher low with a hard $58.50 stop [21, 24]. Second, shares can reclaim $73.50 on at least 1.25x average volume—clearing both the 30-week SMA ($71.94) and 200-day SMA ($72.55)—as S&P 500 breadth exits its Downtrend [21, 23, 24]. Until either trigger fires, patience protects capital.

Note how the pivot ladder frames this waiting period. Overhead resistance sits at Pivot R1 ($70.21) and Pivot R2 ($75.16), right above the 200-day moving average ($72.55) [21, 24]. Every bounce toward $70.21 has met institutional supply so far. Below current levels, the $64.04 52-week low and Pivot S1 ($62.17) form the primary demand shelf, while Pivot S2 ($59.08) sits just above our $58.50 invalidation stop [21, 24]. Respecting those exact levels keeps risk strictly bounded.

In short, both the equity chart and the options chain point to the same conclusion. Implied volatility at 37.5% makes unhedged calls expensive in a Stage 4 tape [24]. Waiting for $64.04 stabilization lets us enter either common shares at 3.54:1 asymmetry or the defined-risk $67.5/$77.5 Bull Call Debit Spread with capped downside [24].

book_paragraphs: If Chapter 7 gave you the fundamental case for why Uber looks cheap at 13.48 times free cash flow, Chapter 8 is here to protect your wallet from buying a falling knife too early. When you and I open Uber's chart on November 17, 2026, the price of $68.81 sits in what Stan Weinstein defines as a Stage 4 markdown. The stock is down 25.84% from its 52-week high of $92.78 and 24.64% over the trailing twelve months. More importantly, it trades below every major trendline that institutional funds use to define technical health: -0.72% below the 50-day simple moving average at $69.31, -0.91% below the 10-week exponential moving average at $69.44, -4.35% below the 30-week simple moving average at $71.94, and -5.16% below the 200-day simple moving average at $72.55.

Look closely at the volume and momentum clues across the weekly, daily, and 4-hour timeframes. On November 17, Uber fell 1.69% on 22.22 million shares—1.27 times its 30-day average volume of 17.53 million shares. When a stock drops on heavier-than-average volume while sitting beneath declining intermediate averages, it tells you that large institutions are still supplying stock into minor rallies rather than quietly accumulating. Meanwhile, the Relative Strength Index sits at 49.11 on the daily chart, 44.99 on the weekly chart, and 48.38 on the 4-hour chart, with a 14-day Average True Range of $2.08 and Bollinger Band width of 10.84%. There is no oversold capitulation washout yet, and no 4-hour bullish reversal turn.

Now zoom out to the macro tape, because no stock trades in a vacuum. As of November 17, 2026, the broader US equity market is in a confirmed Downtrend: only 42.6% of S&P 500 constituents trade above their 50-day moving average, the index has logged 7 distribution days over the past 25 sessions, and the 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to 5.12% (with the 2-year at 4.83%). In a market Downtrend with rising yields, buying a Stage 4 stock at $68.81 means fighting both the company's own trend and the market's tide.

Where does the chart tell us buyers should step up? Below current prices, Uber has a major 52-week low shelf at $64.04, followed by Pivot S1 at $62.17 and Pivot S2 at $59.08. Overhead, Pivot R1 sits at $70.21 and Pivot R2 at $75.16. That geometry gives us two clean, disciplined paths to deploy fresh capital: first, wait for price to test the $62.00 to $65.00 support zone, dry up on selling volume, and form a higher low with a hard invalidation stop at $58.50; or second, wait for Uber to reclaim $73.50 on at least 1.25x average volume, proving it has cleared the 200-day moving average and re-entered Stage 2.

Our deterministic options scan confirms this exact patience. With 30-day implied volatility at 37.5% running hot against 20-day historical volatility of 32.0%, option premiums are elevated and buying naked short-dated calls right now is a losing theta trap. If—and only if—Uber tests its $64.04 support shelf and stabilizes, the optimal defined-risk trade is the January 15, 2027 (59 DTE) $67.5/$77.5 Bull Call Debit Spread. You buy the $67.5 Call at $4.83 mid and sell the $77.5 Call at $1.10 mid for a net debit of $3.73 per share ($373.00 maximum loss), targeting $627.00 maximum profit (1.68-to-1 reward-to-risk) with a $71.23 breakeven, +$36.10 net delta, and just -$1.25 per day in time decay.

Finally, let us audit the 5 existing December 17, 2027 LEAPS contracts already in the portfolio: 4 contracts of the $110 Call ($1,307.91 market value) and 1 contract of the $100 Call ($467.95 market value), totaling $1,775.86 or 2.14% of net worth. Because those contracts carry 395 days of time runway, daily theta decay is minimal. We rate both LEAPS lines a disciplined HOLD as long as Uber defends its $63.00 structural invalidation floor, while strictly refusing to average down until Stage 2 structure returns.

To put this technical discipline into practice, notice how every piece of our chart and options toolkit points to the exact same conclusion. There is no need to predict the exact day that institutional selling stops. Whether Uber drifts down to test its $64.04 shelf and builds a quiet Stage 1 base, or surges back above $73.50 on heavy accumulation volume to reclaim its 200-day moving average, the tape will tell us when the odds have shifted back in our favor. Until that confirmation arrives, standing aside in cash is the highest-conviction move on the board.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: WHY CHEAP STOCKS STILL NEED A FLOOR
book_callouts.text: Fundamental value tells you what a business is worth over three to five years; technical structure tells you who is in control of the order book today. Respecting Stage 4 does not mean doubting Uber's moat—it simply means refusing to subsidize impatient sellers before support is proven.
